files.text:
For most of the nineteenth century a London child with a penny could buy a sheet of a play. Printers off the Strand and in Hoxton engraved the scenes and the characters of the pantomimes and melodramas then on at Covent Garden and Drury Lane, and sold them a penny plain, twopence coloured. You cut them out, pasted them onto card, and set them up in a theatre of wood and paper on the kitchen table.

The stage worked like the real one. The backcloth hung at the back. The wings stood in grooves down each side, one pair behind another, so the scene seemed to go back further than the table did. A ground row stood across the front to hide the floor, and the characters came on from the wings at the end of a wire.

Light came from the front, from a row of small oil lamps or candles in a tin trough along the edge of the stage, and it did what footlights do. Each cut-out threw its shadow up and back onto whatever stood behind it, a little larger than itself, and the nearer it stood to the lamps the larger its shadow was.

Robert Louis Stevenson wrote about the sheets in 1884, in an essay called A Penny Plain and Twopence Coloured, long after the shop where he had bought them as a boy in Edinburgh. What he remembered best was not the plays but the sheets themselves, and the buying of them.

# paper-theatre A Victorian toy theatre set in front of you as you scroll. The stage opens empty, a bare back wall inside the proscenium. Then it is set the way the paper theatres sold "a penny plain, twopence coloured" were set on a kitchen table: the backcloth let down from the flies, the set piece (a ruined temple on its island) slid on along its groove, a cypress wing pushed in from the left and an oak wing from the right, three swallows lowered on threads, the boatman and the heron pushed on, and the ground row of reeds raised from the slot at the front. Every piece is a card cut out of an engraved sheet: absent until its turn, it comes on from where a stagehand would bring it and stops on its mark. Last the footlights come up, and each card throws its shadow up and back onto the scene behind it, larger and softer the further it stands in front of what it falls on. Scroll back and the stage is struck in reverse. Move the pointer (or tilt the phone) and your eye moves: the near cards slide against the far ones. ```html
``` You can also `import { paperTheatre } from './paper-theatre.js'` and call `paperTheatre(section, { src, mode, runway })`. It returns `destroy()`. ## Options | attribute | option | default | what it does | |---------------|----------|----------|--------------| | `data-src` | `src` | required | The stage JSON: its size (2400 x 1350 units), the wall colour, the backcloth, the footlight (position and depth), and each piece's mark (`x`, `y`, `w`, `h`), depth `z` (0 the backcloth, 1 the front), how it comes on (`left`, `right`, `fly`, `rise`) and its `window` in the scroll. Images are named in it and sit beside it. | | `data-mode` | `mode` | `scroll` | `scroll`: a pinned stage on a runway. `static`: the set stage. | | `data-runway` | `runway` | `440` | Section height in svh. The stage is pinned for `runway - 100` svh of travel. | The schedule (fractions of the runway): the empty stage to 0.04, backcloth 0.04-0.16, temple 0.16-0.27, cypress 0.27-0.37, oak 0.37-0.47, swallows 0.47-0.58 (one after another), boat 0.58-0.68, heron 0.68-0.78, reeds 0.78-0.88, footlights 0.90-0.98. Each piece has its own turn, so on a phone the camera can follow it. Events (bubbling, for sound later): `paper-theatre:piece` with `detail: { name, enter }` as each piece starts to come on while scrolling forward, `paper-theatre:lamps` when the footlights come up, and `paper-theatre:done` when the stage is set. ## The real thing - **The sheets.** From about 1811 London printers (West, then Skelt, Webb and Pollock, the last in Hoxton) engraved the scenes and characters of the plays then running and sold them a penny plain, twopence coloured. The buyer cut them out, pasted them on card and stood them on a wooden stage. Ours are "penny plain": one ink, green, on cream. - **How a stage is set.** The backcloth hangs at the back. Wings stand in grooves down each side, so the scene seems deeper than the stage is. Set pieces stand between them, a ground row hides the floor at the front, and the characters come on from the wings on slides or wires. - **The cut.** A card cut out with scissors keeps a thin margin of the white paper round the printed line and is cut in short straight snips. Pockets of paper too small to bother with stay in. - **Footlights.** A row of small lamps or candles along the front edge. A card's shadow is its outline projected from the lamp onto what stands behind it, so it is a little larger than the card and sits above it, and its edge is softer the larger the gap between the card and what the shadow falls on. Simplified: every shadow is projected onto the backcloth's plane (drawn in depth order it still darkens the cards behind, but with the cloth's geometry); the lamps are one point light with a baked penumbra; the cards stop dead on their marks (they don't rock in their grooves or swing on their threads); no characters speak and nothing is coloured (a "twopence coloured" ending was tried and taken out: the plain print reads better; the script is kept in the kit). ## How it works **Offline (Python, in `tools/watercolour-kit/paper-theatre/`; the full-size cut flats are in `library/ornaments/midjourney/theatre/`).** 1. *The sheets.* Each flat was generated on Midjourney on its own sheet of plain paper with the master scene as a style reference, so every card shares one hand and one ink (prompts in `assets/credits.json`). 2. *The cut* (`cutout.py`). The paper colour is read from the sheet's edges and each pixel's optical density against it, `D = -ln(colour / paper)`, says what is ink. Strokes closer than about 9 px are joined into one shape (a morphological close), specks are dropped, enclosed paper smaller than 0.4% of the sheet stays, larger openings are cut out. The shape is grown by a 7 px paper margin, smoothed, traced, and simplified into short straight segments (the snips), then filled at 4x and downsampled for an anti-aliased edge. Pieces that stand in a groove get a straight base, cut where three quarters of their columns already end. A sheet with several pieces (the swallows) is split into one card each. Where Midjourney drew background in the same ink (hatched clouds and hills behind the temple; the reeds running off both ends of their sheet), a few hand-placed polygons leave it outside the cut, the way flower-border uses polygons for what its colour rule misses. 3. *The stage* (`export_theatre.py`). Each card is placed on a 2400 x 1350 stage, scaled to 1.2x its drawn size (never above its source), and saved as RGBA WebP. Its shadow sprite is its silhouette at half size, blurred by a penumbra of `3 + 140 (k - 1)` stage px, where `k = Lz / (Lz - z)` is how much the lamp enlarges it. `stage.json` holds the marks and schedule, `scene.webp` the set stage drawn with the same geometry (the no-JS and reduced-motion picture). **In the browser.** One Canvas 2D, no WebGL. - Scroll is followed on a critically damped spring (quicker going back). Each piece's position is a pure function of that progress: absent before its window, then pushed along its path with an ease-in-out (a hand starts gently and slows onto the mark). - Depth: the eye offset (pointer, or `tilt.js` on a phone) moves each layer by `(1 - z)`, so the backcloth moves most and the front ground row least against the proscenium. The backcloth is drawn 6% oversize so its edges never show. - Shadows: before each card, its sprite is drawn scaled by `k` about the lamp's position and offset to match, at an opacity that rises when the footlights come up. The lamps also warm the bottom of the stage and dim the top a little. - Camera: on a wide screen, the whole proscenium. On a phone (narrow and tall) it goes in until the opening fills about 60% of the screen height, pans sideways to the piece being set, and pulls back to 1.25x for the footlights. It is a function of scroll only, smoothed along it. - Everything outside the opening is clipped, so a wing waiting in the wings is really offstage. The opening gets a fine double rule. ## Theming | variable | default | used for | |---------------|-----------------|----------| | `--paper` | `#f3f0e8` | the page round the stage | | `--pt-gutter` | `var(--gutter)` | side padding of the stage (the demo uses 5px on phones) | | `--pt-runway` | set by the script | section height in scroll mode | The back wall colour, the stage size and the lamp are in `stage.json`. ## Accessibility and motion - Without JS, or with reduced motion, the set stage is an ``. The canvas is `aria-hidden`; the art is ornament (`alt=""`), credits are in `assets/credits.json`. - If reduced motion is switched on mid-visit, the animation stops and the picture shows. - Phone: the stage has `touch-action: pan-y`, a swipe always scrolls, and tilt moves the eye once iOS has asked (first tap). - No UI and no captions on the page; the piece is driven by scroll. ## Cost - Assets 3.45 MB: backcloth 1.2 MB, the oak 0.5 MB, the other cards 0.01-0.3 MB each, shadows a few KB each, the picture 0.6 MB, JSON 3 KB. The cards are 1.2x their drawn size, which is sharp up to about a 1,400 px wide stage at 2x; the Midjourney sheets (1,800-3,800 px) were not upscaled. - One canvas, about twenty image draws a frame. A frame draws only while the scroll spring or the eye is moving and the section is on screen (IntersectionObserver); a phone with tilt active keeps drawing while the section is visible. DPR capped at 2. ## Credits All the art is Connor's, generated on Midjourney (see `assets/credits.json` for each prompt and job). The cutting, placing, shadows and runtime are ours. `tilt.js` is the house helper.
